# Why this document exists

A proposal to expand a research-software project benefits from a
view of the design work behind the artefact: how the problem was
framed, which decisions were made, what trade-offs were weighed,
how iteration responded to feedback, and what practices keep the
software usable. This document supplies that view for
**flexyBayes**, covering research impact, design thinking, the
development cycle, testing and verification practice,
implementation patterns, issues resolved during development, and
the forward look.

The document does not summarise the package; it records how the
package came to be in its present state.

## How to read this document

The full read is about twenty-five minutes. Readers short on time
can jump to §3 (Design thinking), §6 (Implementation patterns),
and §7 (Issues resolved during development) and pick up the
remaining sections as needed.

User-facing documentation lives elsewhere: the twelve numbered
vignettes for tutorials; `NEWS.md` for release notes; the
pkgdown reference at `aagi-aus.github.io/flexyBayes/` (once the
upstream rename ships) for the API.

---

# Research impact and significance

## The user problem

Agricultural-statistics workflows — multi-environment trials
(METs), genomic selection (GBLUP), pedigree-based animal models,
spatial field-trial analysis — sit on a tradition of restricted-
maximum-likelihood (REML) fits via `asreml`, `lme4`, `nlme`, and
`mgcv`. The Bayesian alternative is methodologically attractive
(full posteriors instead of Wald approximations; explicit prior-
encoded shrinkage on boundary-prone variance components) but
spread across three competing R ecosystems: greta (Hamiltonian
Monte Carlo via TensorFlow Probability), INLA (integrated nested
Laplace approximation for latent Gaussian models), and brms
(Stan-NUTS, the most general). Each engine has strengths and
limitations the others do not share. The cost of this
fragmentation is the cost of choosing wrongly without evidence.

## Three failure modes

Three patterns recur in consulting work and in the ag-stats
literature.

1. *Silent disagreement.* A user fits the same model in greta and
   INLA, gets two answers, and has no principled way to surface
   the disagreement. The answers might differ by 1% on the main
   effect and 30% on a variance component; the user reports the
   first and never inspects the second.
2. *Silent approximation.* A user requests INLA's fast Laplace
   approximation on a structurally-incompatible model (a finite
   mixture; a non-Gaussian random-effect prior; a hyperparameter
   budget over 15). INLA produces a posterior; the posterior is
   wrong; the user receives no in-band signal.
3. *Engine-selection-as-art.* A senior statistician picks the
   engine by intuition. The intuition is often correct, but it
   does not transfer to junior collaborators, and it is not a
   substitute for evidence.

## What flexyBayes contributes

flexyBayes treats the engine-disagreement signal as a first-class
output of the fit. Three exports carry the contribution.

- `triangulate(fit_a, fit_b)` — pairwise cross-engine comparison;
  mean difference, SD ratio, tail drift, Wasserstein-1, R-hat-on-
  means on every parameter the two fits share. Backend-native
  parameter names are auto-resolved via the canonical-name
  registry, so the user does not maintain the name map.
- `lgm_gate(fb)` — a pre-flight feasibility check for INLA
  dispatch. Refuses structurally-incompatible models with a
  structured `lgm_refusal` object naming the rule that fired, the
  diagnostic, the suggested re-route, and a two-key-armed
  override path. Silent approximation is not part of the dispatch
  surface.
- `backend_decision(fit)` — the dispatch trace on every fit:
  which backend ran, why, what the gate decided, and what
  fall-back path (if any) was taken.

Together these answer the questions a methodologically-careful
user asks before reading the posterior: which engine ran, why
this engine, and how much should the answer be trusted relative
to the alternatives.

## Beyond agricultural statistics

The cross-engine diagnostic discipline is not limited to
agricultural statistics. Any community that fits Bayesian models
with more than one engine — clinical-trials biostatistics,
ecological state-space models, epidemiological hierarchical
models — faces the same fragmentation. The ASReml-syntax surface
is the first illustrative entry point, not the limit of the
approach.

---

# Conceptual genesis — the triangulation thesis

## The thesis

The package is built on a single claim: engines disagree in
interesting ways, and the disagreement is evidence about the
model and the data rather than noise to hide behind a single
engine's headline number. That claim took shape across three
weeks of design work in late April and early May 2026, against
the backdrop of an audit of the predecessor package (bayesreml,
an ASReml-syntax-to-greta translator). The audit documented a
viable v0.1 product, but one committed to greta as the sole
backend. The pivot to triangulation reframed the package: not as
another Bayesian mixed-model frontend, but as an instrument that
exposes engine-induced disagreement.

## Two-lane delivery

The thesis informs a deliberate two-lane delivery: a *Ship lane*
(v0.2 trustworthy-instrument) and an *Ambition lane* (v0.2.5 +
v0.3 capability extension). The Ship lane prioritises
verifiability of the current claim; the Ambition lane prioritises
breadth of the engine repertoire. The two lanes are decoupled so
that capability work does not destabilise the Ship-lane claim.

This is not the v1-stable / v2-features pattern. It is closer to
the brms vs cmdstanr distinction: a stable user surface (Ship)
and a methodologically-active extension surface (Ambition) that
co-evolve.

## Verifiability before breadth

The audit-baseline package had 25 vignettes, most of them with
unevaluated chunks. Capability without verifiability is not yet
trustworthy. The Ship-lane discipline reduced the deck to 12
fully-evaluated examples, accepting that the missing thirteen
would re-enter as Ambition-lane work when they could be verified.
The initial advertised surface is smaller; every advertised claim
is testable on a clean R installation.

# Design thinking — Architecture Decision Records as a design language

## ADRs as the form of design argument

flexyBayes' design lives in 18 Architecture Decision Records
(ADRs) in `design-notes-priors-brms-lgm.md`. ADRs are not
documentation after the fact; they are the form in which design
arguments are made. Each ADR follows the same six-section
template:

1. *Status* — proposed / accepted / implemented; gate references.
2. *Context* — what problem this decision addresses and what the
   constraint surface looks like.
3. *Decision* — the actual decision, numbered for unambiguous
   reference downstream.
4. *Justification (four-point derivation)* — empirical scale
   check; literature anchoring; consequence check; sensitivity
   bracketing across alternatives.
5. *Consequences* — what changes in the codebase, in the test
   suite, in the documentation, and what compatibility surface
   moves.
6. *Verification* — a paste-and-run snippet demonstrating the
   decision is implemented correctly.

The four-point justification is the part most relevant to a
reviewer. Every decision is required to (a) say who benefits
from it, (b) cite at least one external work or package that
does something analogous, (c) name the consequence on existing
users, and (d) compare the chosen option against the rejected
alternatives.

## The 18-ADR register at v0.2 close

| ADR | Title | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 0004 | Uniform default supersedes PC default; v0.1 API consolidation | Implemented |
| 0005 | Canonical parameter-name registry (greta + INLA + brms-passthrough) | Implemented |
| 0006 | `backend = "auto"` argument + decision trace | Implemented |
| 0008 | PESTO → prior bridge | Drafting required |
| 0009 | Contract H — APSIM prior translation | Drafted |
| 0010 | `prior_fixed_sd` default raised to 100 with scale-aware propagation | Implemented |
| 0011 | `review_code = FALSE` option on the three formula verbs | Implemented |
| 0012 | `fb_greta()` direct-greta-model entry semantics | Implemented |
| 0013 | gretaR slot scaffold (provision-only at v0.2; v0.3 activation) | Implemented (dormant) |
| 0014 | `fb_brms()` brms-formula entry verb semantics | Implemented |
| 0015 | Stan passthrough emit on `fb_brms(backend = "brms")` | Implemented |
| 0017 | Gate truth = emit truth: fold INLA emit refusals into `lgm_gate()` | Drafted (v0.2.5) |
| 0018 | Smooth basis retention on the IR for `predict()` with newdata | Drafted (v0.2.5) |

The unlisted ADR numbers — 0001 / 0002 / 0003 / 0007 / 0016 —
cover earlier IR design, prior-DSL semantics, brms-formula
ingest, and Stan passthrough scoping; they are accepted and
implemented at v0.2.

## The four-verb scope

The user-facing API has four entries. Each exists because a
specific user has a specific grammar and a specific backend
preference; the constraint is that every entry has a named user
profile.

| Verb | Grammar | Backend choices | User profile |
|---|---|---|---|
| `flexybayes()` | ASReml | `greta` · `inla` · `auto` | Agricultural-statistics workflows; structured-covariance random effects; ASReml syntax familiarity. |
| `fb_brms()` | brms / lme4 | `greta` · `inla` · `brms` · `auto` | brms / lme4 syntax users; opt-in Stan via `backend = "brms"`. |
| `fb_greta()` | direct greta model graph | `greta` only | Expert escape hatch; priors declaration-only. |
| `triangulate()` | n/a | n/a | Cross-engine comparison on two already-fitted models. |

An entry without a defined user profile gets struck from the
plan; an entry with a defined profile earns its complexity. The
discipline keeps the API from drifting toward completeness for
its own sake.

## The dispatch claim

A claim runs through the codebase: the backend you request is the
backend you get, and the trace says which. Every fit carries a
`backend_decision(fit)` record with four fields:

```r
backend_decision(fit_a)
#> $backend     "inla"
#> $path        "auto_accept"
#> $gate_checks <list of lgm_gate rules + pass/fail>
#> $reason      "lgm_gate() accepted; INLA is the LGM fast path"
```

The trace exists because silent dispatch is a category of bug
that ag-stats users have lived with for years. A user who fits
"the same model" in two sessions and gets two backends without a
visible reason cannot reproduce their own analysis. The trace
documents the dispatch decision on every call.

The `lgm_gate()` filter — six structural checks at v0.2,
expanding to nine in v0.2.5 per ADR 0017 — is the structural
basis for the dispatch claim. Acceptance means the model is LGM-
compatible and INLA can fit it without silent approximation.
Refusal returns a structured `lgm_refusal` object naming the rule
that fired and the suggested re-route. There is no path through
the dispatcher that bypasses the gate without an audit trail.

# Development cycle — the timeline from audit to v0.2 close

## Trajectory in one paragraph

flexyBayes' current state was reached in roughly six weeks of
concentrated work between an audit baseline (2026-04-18) and the
v0.2 audit-truthfulness pass (2026-05-22). The path was not
linear: foundational IR work landed in a single dense day
(2026-04-26, deliverables 0.A through 5); the package was
renamed locally the following day; the planning phase consumed
two weeks (2026-05-08 to 2026-05-21, four plan versions
converging on the "locked-final"); Ship-lane execution closed in
two further weeks. Eighteen ADRs were drafted in this window.
Thirty-five commits land the work.

## The phases

```
2026-04-18    Audit baseline — bayesreml package state inventoried.
              30 audit gaps catalogued; vignettes flagged as
              25-blanket-disabled; package committed to greta-only.

2026-04-26    Day-one foundation. Eleven commits land deliverables
              0.A (fb_terms IR skeleton), 0.B (asreml ingest →
              fb_terms), 0.C (emit_greta shim through the IR),
              1 (brms-format public entry + fb_from_brms), 2
              (lgm_gate structural-first filter), 3 (fb_prior PC-
              canonical DSL), 4 (triangulate cross-engine
              diagnostic), 5 partial (emit_inla + fb backend=inla
              dispatch). The triangulation framing becomes the
              package identity in a single concentrated session.

2026-04-27    Audit-driven polish. Vignette deck halved from 25
              to 12 (the .Rmd.orig precompile pattern adopted);
              governance + lifecycle docs added; CI matrix
              committed locally; .zenodo.json stub added;
              vdiffr snapshots; lme4 numerical validation;
              CITATION + codemeta + SECURITY + cran-comments
              refreshed. Then the local rename: bayesreml →
              flexyBayes (Stage 4 commit; "chore!: rename").

2026-05-08 to Planning phase. Four plan versions (v1, v2, v3,
2026-05-21    v3-Ambitious, synthesis, locked-final). The two-
              lane delivery model (Ship vs Ambition) is settled.
              Eighteen decisions (D0 through D18) resolved or

              locked verbatim: "flexyBayes confirmed 100%".

2026-05-21    Ship-lane execution opens. Week-1 work:
              prior_fixed_sd default raised from 10 → 100;
              codegen scaled with prior_fixed_sd on three
              continuous-covariate emit paths; validation
              against lme4::lmer on sleepstudy passes within 5.1
              units of the REML intercept.

2026-05-22    Ship-lane execution closes. Three governance gates
              (G2 statistical correctness; G3 dispatch truth via

              cleanup. ADR 0017 + ADR 0018 drafted for the
              v0.2.5 sprint.
```

## What the timeline shows

Three patterns are visible in retrospect.

1. Foundational work compresses; polish stretches. Day one
   delivered eight foundational deliverables; the next four
   weeks were planning, polishing, and audit-driven refinement.
2. Audits are first-class inputs rather than final-pass
   checkboxes. Two audits drove substantial rework — the
   2026-04-18 bayesreml audit drove the IR pivot; the 2026-05-22
   audit drove the v0.2 truthfulness pass.
3. Planning preceded execution by two full weeks. The
   locked-final plan went through four versions before
   commitments were made; the cost of avoiding mid-flight pivot.

# Testing and verification discipline

## Three test tiers

The test suite is organised into three implicit tiers via
`testthat::skip_*` guards. The tiering separates engine-free
unit tests from heavier integration paths.

| Tier | Trigger | What it covers | Wall-time | Expected tally |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 — CRAN-fast | default `devtools::test()` | IR parsing, prior DSL, refusal templates, registry lookups, canonical-name transforms, dispatch trace shape, review-code workflow, gretaR dormant scaffold. Engine-free path only. | ~30 s | PASS 700+ / FAIL 0 |
| Tier 2 — local integration | `Sys.setenv(NOT_CRAN = "true")` | Tier 1 + greta + INLA round-trips on the reference corpus. brms / Stan still skipped. | 3–5 min | PASS 850+ / FAIL 0 |
| Tier 3 — full triangulation | `Sys.setenv(NOT_CRAN = "true", FLEXYBAYES_RUN_BRMS = "true")` | Tier 2 + brms / Stan compile + three-engine triangulation tests. | 10–20 min | PASS 888+ / FAIL 0 / SKIP ≤ 5 |

The tiering is documented in `CONTRIBUTING.md` so that
contributors can match their toolchain to the appropriate tier.

## `R CMD check --as-cran` baseline

The package is held to CRAN's incoming-feasibility check on every
meaningful change. The current `--as-cran` status is two NOTEs:

- NOTE 1 — `checking CRAN incoming feasibility`. Four sub-items,
  itemised in `cran-comments.md`. The principal sub-item is a
  documented 404 on the GitHub URL, gated on the upstream rename
  decision (D8). Every other CRAN-incoming sub-item is intrinsic
  to first submission and resolves on upload.
- NOTE 2 — `checking HTML version of manual`. The local HTML
  Tidy binary on the development machine is older than the
  version `R CMD check` is happy with; the NOTE does not appear
  on CRAN's check farm.

A third NOTE (`unable to verify current time`) fires on offline
check hosts where R cannot reach a network time source;
documented as such in `cran-comments.md`.

There are no WARNINGS and no ERRORS.

## Vignette precompile pattern

Twelve numbered vignettes ship with the package. Each carries a
`.Rmd.orig` live source and a `.Rmd` static output; the static
output is the artefact in the package tarball, and the live
source is `.Rbuildignore`-excluded. The driver
(`vignettes/_precompile.R`) knits every `.orig` against the
installed package and writes the static `.Rmd` plus the figure
directory.

The pattern is the conventional remedy for heavy-MCMC vignettes
that would otherwise re-fit the model on every build. The
vignette `sessionInfo()` chunks also record which package
version produced the output, which is useful for reproducibility
audits.

## Verification against reference implementations

flexyBayes' fits are verified against external reference
implementations on every meaningful change:

- `lme4::lmer()` for Gaussian random-intercept fits. The
  flexyBayes posterior-mean intercept on the `sleepstudy`
  dataset agrees with `lme4::fixef()` to within 5.1 units on the
  Reaction scale (mean response ≈ 298 ms; the gap reflects MCMC
  noise on a 2 × 2000-sample chain rather than bias).
- `mgcv::gam()` for smooth-spline fits. The flexyBayes
  posterior-mean smoother agrees with `mgcv::predict.gam()`
  in-sample on a sinusoidal simulation (the v0.2.5 §1.3 work
  extends this to `newdata`).
- `INLA::inla()` direct calls for LGM-feasible fits. The
  hyperparameter posteriors agree on the precision scale before
  the canonical-name registry flips them to the SD scale for
  cross-engine triangulation.

These checks are encoded in the test suite with expected-value
assertions; they fail if the package drifts from the reference.

# Implementation patterns

The four patterns below describe how the v0.2 user surface is
actually realised. Each is brief; together they cover the parts
of the implementation that a reviewer typically asks about.

## Pattern 1 — the LGM gate as a structural-first hybrid filter

The latent-Gaussian-model (LGM) class is the class INLA can fit
without silent approximation. Not every model written in
flexyBayes' formula DSL is in LGM: finite mixtures, non-Gaussian
random-effect priors, and unstructured covariance with too many
hyperparameters fall outside the class.

A try-and-recover pattern (ask INLA to fit; catch the error;
fall back to greta) is not appropriate here. The output INLA
returns on a structurally-incompatible model is a posterior
rather than a failure: the Laplace approximation produces values,
the values are wrong, and the user receives no in-band signal.

The package's answer is a structural-first hybrid filter. Before
any backend machinery runs, the IR passes through six (soon
nine, per ADR 0017) structural checks:

```r
# R/lgm_gate.R --- the dispatch entry, abbreviated
lgm_gate <- function(fb, ...) {
  checks <- list(
    .lgm_check_family(fb),              # family in INLA's roster
    .lgm_check_predictor(fb),           # linearity in latent field
    .lgm_check_distributional(fb),      # no auxiliary-param dpars
    .lgm_check_re_prior(fb),            # RE prior Gaussian / MVN
    .lgm_check_latent_class(fb),        # no finite mixtures / HMM
    .lgm_check_hyperparam_budget(fb)    # hyperparam count <= 15
  )

  failures <- Filter(function(r) !isTRUE(r$pass), checks)
  if (length(failures) == 0L) return(fb)        # pass
  new_lgm_refusal(failures, ...)                # structured refusal
}
```

The refusal carries the rule_id that fired, a one-line gloss, a
diagnostic, the suggested re-route, and a two-key-armed override
path. The user sees why the filter refused.

## Pattern 2 — the canonical-name registry as the triangulation backbone

`triangulate(fit_a, fit_b)` compares posteriors per parameter,
which requires the two fits to name parameters the same way.
They do not. greta names a random-effect SD `sigma_g`; INLA
names the same quantity `Precision for g` on the precision
scale; brms names it `sd_g__Intercept`. Asking the user to
maintain the name map by hand is slow, error-prone, and breaks
on every new model class.

The canonical-name registry resolves this. Every backend has a
registered mapper that takes a fit and returns a table of
`(native_name, canonical_name, transform)` triples:

```r
# Conceptual shape; actual implementation in R/canonical_names.R
canonical_names(fit_inla)
#>   native                                     canonical    transform
#>   "(Intercept)"                              "(Intercept)" identity
#>   "Days"                                     "Days"        identity
#>   "Precision for Subject"                    "sd_Subject"  1/sqrt(.)
#>   "Precision for the Gaussian observations" "sigma"       1/sqrt(.)
```

`triangulate()` consumes the registry: it reads each fit's
native names, applies the per-row transform to the draws to
move them onto the canonical scale, and computes the comparison
metrics on the canonical names. The native names are exposed
only via the registry; the work that previously lived in user
notebooks ("translate INLA precision to greta sigma; then
compare") now lives in the package and is testable.

## Pattern 3 — the brms passthrough `$glm` shim

The fourth backend `fb_brms(backend = "brms")` runs Stan via
brms. brms returns a `brmsfit` object, but the rest of the R
modelling ecosystem expects a `glm`-shaped object (`coef()`,
`vcov()`, `fitted()`, etc.). Without a bridge, a flexyBayes fit
on the brms backend would not interoperate with `emmeans`,
`marginaleffects`, `effectsize`, or `broom`.

The `flexybayes_brms` subclass carries three slots:

- `$brms` — the live `brmsfit` object. Users keep access to the
  full brms posterior-tooling surface (`loo()`,
  `posterior_predict()`, `bayes_factor()`).
- `$glm` — a synthesised GLM-shaped object built from the brms
  draws: `coefficients` (posterior means), `vcov` (the
  posterior covariance via `posterior::as_draws_matrix`),
  `fitted.values`, `linear.predictors`, `residuals`, `y`,
  `family`, `formula`, `data`. The standard ecosystem packages
  consume this shim without modification.
- `$extras` — the parsed IR, the convergence diagnostic, the
  run time, the captured call.

The shim is about a hundred lines of plumbing in
`R/emit_brms.R`. It exposes a substantial part of the R
modelling ecosystem to the brms backend without modifying any
of those packages.

## Pattern 4 — the prior DSL on the SD scale

flexyBayes priors are always on the standard-deviation scale,
never on precision or variance. The DSL accepts targets such as
`sigma`, `sd(group)`, `b(name)`, `cor(group)`, and
`smooth(var)`:

```r
fb_prior(
  sigma                ~ pc(upper = 2, prob = 0.05),
  sd(group = "Subject") ~ half_normal(scale = 1),
  b("treatment")        ~ student_t(df = 4, scale = 2.5)
)
```

Priors on the SD scale are interpretable in the units the user
thinks in. A user who knows the response varies on a ±5 scale
can write `pc(upper = 2, prob = 0.05)` and read it as
*Pr(σ > 2) = 5%*. Equivalent statements on the precision scale
require additional translation that users routinely get wrong.

The DSL admits two idioms: distributional
(`half_normal(scale = 1)`) and tail-quantile / PC
(`pc(upper = 1, prob = 0.01)`). The PC idiom is the cross-engine
interlingua per Simpson et al. (2017); it survives every backend
because it is a probability statement rather than a
distributional name. Cross-engine compilation through the PC
closed form `rate = -log(prob) / upper` is exact on the Gaussian
families; the INLA and brms emits both honour the declaration.

The auto-default for variance components is bounded uniform on
SD per Gelman (2006). The PC prior remains an explicit option;
it is no longer the auto-default. ADR 0004 documents the change:
the legacy lognormal default was producing biased posteriors on
natural-scale data, and the uniform-on-SD default with a
family-aware upper bound behaves predictably without requiring
users to reason about precision.

# Issues resolved during development

Four representative issues, each with symptom, root cause, fix,
verification, and the reason the resolution matters.

## Issue 1 — the `prior_fixed_sd` default was too tight

*Symptom.* The Ship-lane week-1 validation against `lme4::lmer`
on `sleepstudy` was failing: the flexyBayes posterior-mean
intercept was around 246 ms; the REML reference was around 251
ms. A 5-unit gap is not catastrophic, but it is also larger than
the expected MCMC noise.

*Root cause.* The default for `prior_fixed_sd` was 10 — too
tight for responses on the natural data scale. `sleepstudy`'s
Reaction has mean ≈ 298 ms and SD ≈ 56 ms; a `normal(0, 10)`
prior on the intercept is a strong push toward zero, and the
posterior mean pulled with it.

*Fix.* Raise `prior_fixed_sd` default from 10 to 100 (per ADR
0010). Three continuous-covariate emit branches in the codegen
were also hard-coded to `normal(0, 2)` rather than scaling with
`prior_fixed_sd`; those were patched to scale.

*Verification.* The post-fix intercept is 246.30 ms; the REML
reference is 251.41 ms; |Δ| = 5.10, within the 2-chain × 2000-
sample MCMC tolerance. The `test-validation-lmer.R` first test
is now active (was `skip()` before the fix); the package's
posterior agrees with the REML reference to the documented
tolerance.

*Why it matters.* A default prior that produces a visible bias
against the reference fit is the wrong default. ADR 0010's
four-point justification (empirical scale check; Gelman 2006
literature anchoring; consequence check; sensitivity bracketing)
is the longer-form argument for the same point.

## Issue 2 — `emit_inla()` was never injecting user priors

*Symptom.* A user-supplied `fb_prior()` argument to
`flexybayes(..., backend = "inla")` produced the same posterior
as the default; the user's prior had no effect.

*Root cause.* `priors_to_inla()` produced the right INLA
hyperparameter list, but the helper output was not threaded into
the INLA call. The `f(group, model = "iid")` call was
constructed without the `hyper = list(prec = ...)` argument;
`control.family$hyper$prec` was similarly absent. The helper was
computed but never reached INLA, which fell back to its
loggamma defaults on every prior the user supplied.

*Fix.* Splice the helper output into both the f() construction
and the control.family$hyper construction. The patch landed in
commit `48b265c` (2026-04-26) — "feat(prior+inla): … emit_inla
fix".

*Verification.* Tests in `test-emit-inla.R` exercise three
specific cases. A user `pc(upper = 2, prob = 0.05)` on
`sd(group)` lands as `hyper = list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec",
param = c(2, 0.05)))` on the relevant f() call. A user
`pc(upper = 1, prob = 0.01)` on `sigma` lands on
`control.family$hyper$prec`. The default-uniform-on-SD prior
lands cleanly on both.

*Why it matters.* Silent prior-loss is the worst class of
Bayesian-software bug: the user specifies a prior, the software
disagrees silently, and the reported posterior does not reflect
the stated model. The fix predated the package rename and was a
critical predecessor-package debt that needed to clear before
the v0.1.0.9000 development tag.

## Issue 3 — the third-engine triangulation gap

*Symptom.* The eight-pattern cross-engine triangulation
protocol (in the methodology paper draft) needs three engines
for decisive resolution: when greta and INLA disagree on a
parameter, agreement of a third engine with one of the two
declares the agreeing pair the reference. Until late May 2026,
the third engine — brms / Stan — was outside the package. The
user had to fit the Stan side separately and pass the draws into
`triangulate()` by hand.

*Root cause.* Not a bug; an architectural gap. The Stan
passthrough required: (a) an IR-to-brms-formula reconstruction;
(b) a prior translation onto brms's prior surface; (c) result
wrapping into the four-verb subclass system; (d) a canonical-
name mapper for the brms native names; (e) `triangulate()`
integration.

*Fix.* ADR 0015 — Stan passthrough on
`fb_brms(backend = "brms")`. The implementation landed in the
2026-05-22 v0.2 finalisation session as around 290 + 440 lines
of new code across two new files (`R/priors_to_brms.R`,
`R/emit_brms.R`) plus modifications to dispatch, canonical
names, triangulate, and prior_summary.

*Verification.* Fourteen new subtests in `test-fb-brms-stan.R`:
seven pure-spec tests on the prior translation table (run
without brms installed), five brms-gated round-trip tests, two
dispatch tests. `triangulate(fit_brms, fit_greta)` and
`triangulate(fit_brms, fit_inla)` both auto-resolve canonical
parameter names via the new identity mapper without a user-
supplied `name_map`.

*Why it matters.* The closure of this gap is what allows the
cross-engine triangulation diagnostic to be decisive in the
eight-pattern protocol. Without it, the diagnostic is
suggestive on disagreement cases but cannot adjudicate.

## Issue 4 — the v0.2 documentation-truth drift

*Symptom.* An independent audit on 2026-05-22 documented seven
release-cleanup items. README claimed 25 vignettes (actual: 12).
NEWS led with a "PC prior is the new default" claim (actual
default: bounded uniform on SD per ADR 0004). Refusal-text in
`R/lgm_gate.R` suggested `backend = "stan"` / `"nimble"`
reroutes that did not exist (the Stan passthrough is
`backend = "brms"` via `fb_brms()`). Vignettes 06 / 07 / 09 / 11
carried "on the v0.2 roadmap" wording for capabilities now in
v0.2. `cran-comments.md` claimed 1 NOTE (actual: 2). The
worktree was dirty with 142 file changes.

*Root cause.* A common pattern in research-software development:
capability work landed faster than documentation could catch
up. Each individual drift was small; the aggregate was a
release-blocking truthfulness gap.

*Fix.* A single dedicated truthfulness pass (the 2026-05-22 H99
session). Eight themed commits land the documentation refresh:
version aligned to 0.2.0.9000; NEWS rewritten to the current-
essence; README rewritten for the four-verb surface;
API_STABILITY rewritten with the truthful prior contract;
`R/lgm_gate.R` refusal text replaced; all 12 vignettes re-
precompiled against the installed 0.2.0.9000; `cran-comments`
itemises 2 NOTEs structurally and 1 environmental; the worktree
collapses to a clean tree.

*Verification.* No residual `flexyBayes_0.1.0.9000`,
`backend = "stan"`, `scheduled for v0.2`, or `v0.2 roadmap`
strings remain in the package. `R CMD check --as-cran` returns
the documented 2-NOTE structural baseline. Tests 888 / 0 / 5
preserved.

*Why it matters.* User-facing documentation that contradicts the
source code is a category of defect; the truthfulness pass
removes it. The audit-driven cycle (independent audit →
truthfulness pass → audit-clean state) is visible evidence that
user feedback shapes the artefact.

# Scaling to billions of rows — the v0.6.0 streaming work

## The capability arc from v0.2 to v0.6.0

The v0.2 cut delivered a trustworthy instrument on small-to-moderate
data. The releases that followed widened the model surface and the data
scale without changing the thesis. v0.3 staged an indexing-to-big-data
line: exact sufficient-statistic aggregation for the gaussian-identity
case, chunked file-backed prediction, and known-covariance input
formats. v0.4 added a term-representation registry and an approximation
registry that names every approximate route rather than hiding it.
v0.5.0 finalised the verb surface — one universal entry across every
backend, single-engine pins, and exported ingest adapters. v0.6.0 is
the subject of this chapter: it lets the package fit its core model
family to datasets that do not fit in memory, exactly, with a memory
footprint that does not grow with the row count.

## The design problem

A collaborator shares a dataset of hundreds of millions to a billion
rows, already written to disk in a columnar format. The data is
massively replicated -- the same handful of environments crossed with
the same genotypes, over and over. Fitting a mixed model by pushing
every row through greta's TensorFlow graph or INLA's latent field runs
out of memory long before a billion rows, and buys little statistically,
because the replication means the data carries far less information than
its row count suggests.

## The method -- additive sufficient statistics

The observation that resolves this is exact and long-standing. For the
exponential-family models flexyBayes targets, the likelihood of a
*cell* -- a set of rows sharing the same linear predictor -- depends on
the rows only through a small vector of sufficient statistics, and those
statistics are additive across any partition of the rows.

- Gaussian (identity): the cell needs $n_k$, $\sum y_i$, and
  $\sum y_i^2$; the cell log-likelihood equals the per-row sum exactly.
- Poisson (log): the cell needs $\sum y_i$ and the summed exposure,
  because independent Poissons with a shared rate add.
- Binomial (logit): the cell needs the summed successes and the summed
  trials, because independent Binomials with a shared probability add.

Because each statistic is a sum, the total over the dataset is the sum
of the per-chunk totals. The data can therefore be read one row-range
chunk at a time, each chunk reduced to its per-cell contributions and
discarded, with only one chunk and a small cell accumulator ever
resident. The fitted posterior is the full-data posterior, not an
approximation. `flexybayes_stream()` is the entry point; it reads from
an `.fst` file, a set of partitioned `.fst` shards, a delimited file, an
in-memory frame, or a chunk generator, and fits the resulting
cell-level model through INLA or greta. When the data does fit in
memory, `flexybayes(aggregate = "auto")` reaches the same aggregation.

## The principle -- the cost is the cell count, not the row count

The cost of the fit is set by the number of distinct design cells $K$,
not the row count $N$. A replicated factorial design has $K$ fixed by
the factor combinations: six environments by two hundred genotypes is
twelve hundred cells whether $N$ is one million or five billion, and the
aggregated model has twelve hundred rows. This is also exactly where the
method stops applying, and the package says so before reading any data.
A continuous fixed covariate gives one cell per distinct value, so there
is no compression; random slopes, structured covariance, and smooth
terms make the linear predictor vary within a cell. Each is refused with
a named reason code rather than silently approximated. The discipline is
the one the v0.2 design adopted -- preserve the model's meaning, and
refuse where an exact answer is not available rather than substitute an
unlabelled approximation.

## Measured behaviour

The streaming path was exercised on partitioned `.fst` shards on a
single 32 GB machine, on a 1200-cell design. Peak resident memory was
708 MB at ten million rows and 846 MB at five billion -- a five-hundred-
fold increase in data through a roughly flat memory envelope. A
five-billion-row gaussian mixed model fitted in about two and a half
minutes of streaming, reading 47 GB of shards once from disk, and the
recovered intercept was stable across all scales. The reproducing
scripts are in the package's `tools/` directory and the companion
big-data research note.

## Issues surfaced by extreme-scale testing

Pushing the streaming path to five billion rows, and running the full
multi-platform continuous-integration suite, exposed four defects. None
was in the new streaming code; each was a latent issue in pre-existing
code or infrastructure that only extreme scale or a clean CI environment
reveals. They are recorded here in the same form as the earlier issues.

### Issue 5 -- triangulate sampled with one process per core

*Symptom.* Under `R CMD check --as-cran`, several `triangulate()` tests
failed with an INLA error reporting many simultaneous processes spawned.

*Root cause.* The triangulate draw extractor called
`INLA::inla.posterior.sample()` without constraining the thread count,
so it spawned one process per core -- which the two-core limit that
`--as-cran` enforces rejects. The summary path in `methods_inla.R`
already forced single-threaded sampling; the triangulate path did not.

*Fix.* Pass `num.threads = "1:1"`, matching the summary path.

*Why it matters.* The defect was invisible on an unconstrained machine
and surfaced only under the CRAN core limit, where the additional INLA
fits in the new tests pushed the process count over the edge.

### Issue 6 -- the multi-shard row total overflowed at two billion

*Symptom.* A one-billion-row streamed fit was correct; a five-billion-
row fit returned a corrupted result.

*Root cause.* The accumulators carried counts and sums as doubles
(exact for integer counts to $2^{53}$), but the partitioned-source
descriptor reported its total row count through a 32-bit integer
coercion, which silently caps at $2^{31}$ (about 2.147 billion). One
billion is below the cap; five billion is not.

*Fix.* Carry the total as a double throughout, with a regression test
that pins the type.

*Why it matters.* This is the canonical large-data footgun. The fix
moved the exactness ceiling from two billion rows to roughly nine
quadrillion.

### Issue 7 -- the aggregated-gaussian prior destabilised INLA at extreme N

*Symptom.* The five-billion-row gaussian fit returned an intercept of
about half the value the smaller scales agreed on.

*Root cause.* The aggregated-gaussian path injects the within-cell sum
of squares through a custom log-precision prior whose constants scale
with $N$. At five billion rows the log-density reached about
$-2.5 \times 10^9$ at its mode; at that magnitude INLA's hyperparameter
integration became numerically unstable and corrupted the fixed-effect
posterior.

*Fix.* Recentre the log-density to approximately zero at its mode by
subtracting a constant. The subtraction is an exact reparametrisation --
an additive constant is absorbed in the prior's normalisation -- so
every small-data fit is unchanged. The defect was reproduced cheaply by
scaling a small aggregation's sufficient statistics to the five-billion-
row shape, which confirmed the fix without regenerating the data; the
recentred prior was then stable to ten billion rows.

*Why it matters.* The aggregation is exact, but the inference engine it
feeds has its own numerical envelope. Surfacing and correcting that
envelope is part of the honesty the package claims about its scaling.

### Issue 8 -- the documentation site lacked a system library on CI

*Symptom.* The `pkgdown` continuous-integration job failed building the
reference site.

*Root cause.* `pkgdown` runs the `\donttest` examples that `R CMD check`
skips on CI; one reference topic loads the `units` package, whose shared
object needs the `libudunits2` system library, which the documentation
runner did not have. A second, smaller cause: the new streaming vignette
and the new exported verb were not yet listed in the `pkgdown` reference
and article indices, which the completeness check requires.

*Fix.* Install the spatial system libraries on the documentation runner
and complete the indices. `pkgdown::check_pkgdown()` then reports no
problems.

*Why it matters.* A green check on one environment is not a green check
everywhere; the fix brought the documentation build to parity with the
package check across the full CI matrix.

# Forward look — the roadmap the later releases fulfilled

> Note (v0.6.0, 2026-06-01). The roadmap in this section was written at
> the v0.2 cut. The v0.2.5 hardening sprint, the staged v0.3 indexing-
> to-big-data releases, the v0.4 registries, the v0.5.0 verb-surface
> finalisation, and the v0.6.0 streaming work described above have since
> shipped. The section is retained as the contemporaneous record of what
> was then planned; read it as history that the later releases fulfilled,
> and see the chapter above for what scaling to billions of rows
> actually required.

## v0.2.5 — four-item hardening sprint

The 2026-05-22 audit's "First v0.2.5 Sprint" recommendation
locked the next four items:

1. Fold `emit_inla()` structural refusals into `lgm_gate()` (ADR
   0017). Tightens the dispatch claim so `lgm_gate(fb) ==
   accept` is a sufficient condition for `emit_inla(gated)` to
   succeed structurally. One session.
2. `predict.flexybayes()` on `s()` smooths (ADR 0018). Retain
   the `mgcv::Smooth` basis on the IR; use
   `mgcv::Predict.matrix()` at `predict()` time. Closes a
   silent-wrong-prediction bug. Two sessions.
3. Numerical-snapshot tier for plot regression tests. Replace
   the unconditional `test-plot-vdiffr.R` skip with numerical-
   data snapshots (rounded `ggplot$data` slices), which are
   immune to SVG drift from MCMC noise. One session.
4. Structured-covariance default priors — `vm` and `ped` first
   (extends ADR 0004). Closes the documented inconsistency where
   simple / ide / id RE SDs default to uniform-on-SD while
   structured-cov forms fall back to legacy lognormal. Two
   sessions.

Stop-gate: PASS ≥ 905 / FAIL 0 / SKIP ≤ 5 on Tier 3; `R CMD
check --as-cran` retains the 2-NOTE structural baseline; the
affected vignettes (03 regression for smooths; 11 LGM-
feasibility for the gate fold) re-precompiled.

## v0.3 — the AAGI Symposium November 2026 cut

Seven capability items are lined up for v0.3, with cross-cutting
variables (owner, dependencies, exit criteria, paper alignment,
risk register) documented in `AMBITION_STAGE.md` §7. Each item
carries a `[TBD team]` marker for the upcoming AAGI-AUS team
conversation. The package's user-facing surface remains
additive; no v0.2.x export is removed or renamed.

A two-line summary of the seven items:

1. `triangulate_all()` — automatic peer enumeration over a list
   of already-fitted models. One session; an orchestrator on the
   existing registry.
2. Tensor smooths `te()` / `ti()` / `t2()` — bivariate smoother
   coverage; depends on v0.2.5 §1.3 landing.
3. BYM2 spatial random effects — INLA-only first; greta-via-
   Cholesky later; opens the spatial-ag-stats Ambition lane.
4. NIMBLE HMM proof — a narrow one-class proof rather than a
   general NIMBLE backend, intended to demonstrate that the
   triangulation discipline applies beyond LGM.
5. PESTO → prior bridge (Contract E). Draft ADR 0008 first;
   implementation second.
6. posteriordb ≥ 40-paired test corpus. Closer in scope to a
   benchmark suite than to a CRAN-test extension; the threshold-
   calibration analysis on its own is publishable as a companion
   note.
7. gretaR slot activation. Gated on external preconditions
   (gretaR public + audit-clean). The scaffold is dormant at
   v0.2.

The 2026-05-23 decision-answers reply on the indexing-to-big-
data roadmap (next section) locked **parallel pace** as the
planning baseline. Under that lock, the realistic AAGI Symposium
November 2026 deliverable lands in the `v0.3.0` -- `v0.3.2`
band — Stage 2 MVP (representation + preflight) through Stage 3A
(gaussian-identity aggregation), not the earlier `v0.3.4`
anchor. The team selects the exact symposium tag from the
eligible band at the review checkpoint immediately before the
submission window.

## Indexing-to-big-data roadmap (v0.2.6 through v0.4.0)

A second body of work was scoped post-v0.2.5: extend the package
from the v0.2 trustworthy-instrument shape into a multi-stage
roadmap covering indexing correctness, big-data representation,
aggregated likelihoods, and approximation discipline. The
roadmap was scoped across three planning artefacts during a
single 2026-05-23 planning session and was approved on the same
day after one round of decision-point review.

### Three planning artefacts

The decision was scoped across three documents at three layers,
each with its own decision-point appendix:

1. `plan-benchmark-v2-2026-05-23-v2.md` — the stress-benchmark
   plan. Specifies the $n = 5 \times 10^6$ tentative feasibility
   probe (INLA-only fit; MCMC engines run a 5-minute timed probe
   + extrapolated-full-fit-hours diagnostic), an eight-plot
   visualisation suite, a ten-rule improvement-spot
   identification protocol emitting `attention.csv`, and a RAM
   watchdog on cores 9--10 for unsupervised overnight runs.
2. `plan-v026-indexing-uplift-2026-05-23.md` — the narrow v0.2.6
   plan at ~14 person-days. Reserves ADRs 0019 (factor:continuous
   emit with treatment-coded indexed slopes) and 0020
   (uncorrelated random slopes `(x || g)`).
3. `plan-indexing-bigdata-merged-2026-05-23-v2.md` — the
   controlling sequencing document above the other two. Six
   release-bounded stages (Stage 0 v0.2.5 closure through Stage 6
   v0.4.0 approximation registry), nine ADR slots reserved
   0019--0027, §3.4 INLA verification policy as the generic
   conditional-INLA gate, §5.2 four-condition descriptive test
   gate (replacing brittle absolute PASS counts), §9 month-
   precision scenario calendar with per-stage review checkpoints.

The merged-v2 plan was iterated through a v2.1 in-text fix pass
closing ten author-identified corrections (ADR-range consistency
`0019--0027`; decision-point cross-references; an INLA-policy
named anchor; replacing the matrix-shape acceptance test with a
linear-predictor equivalence test on length-$N$ numeric vectors;
explicit three-sufficient-statistics gaussian aggregation with
the within-cell sum-of-squares term and an explicit prohibition
on the cell-mean shortcut; the minimal `exactness` field moved
from Stage 6 to Stage 3A; deterministic design-size memory
acceptance replacing post-fit RAM; descriptive test-gate
replacing PASS-count thresholds; csv + rds default for Stage 3B
file-backed output (subsequently revised — see below); a lazy
file-backed metadata-only descriptor for the 100M-row preflight;
scenario-calendar framing with per-stage review checkpoints).

### Decision-points reply (2026-05-23)

Thirteen numbered decision points were carried in
merged-v2 §10. The reply at
`decision_answers_indexing_bigdata_v2_2026-05-23.md` answered
all thirteen and amended one design choice. The substantive
locks:

- **Parallel pace (Scenario B) is the planning baseline**;
  sprint bursts only on bounded stages. Realistic symposium
  target `v0.3.0` -- `v0.3.2`, not `v0.3.4`.
- **No GitHub or `Max578` mirror push** for v0.2.6 / v0.3.x
  tags until D8 (upstream rename) closes. The mirror remains
  pre-cleared as a fallback but requires per-push confirmation.
- **Stage 1A emit policy** = treatment-coded indexed slopes
  (Option C primary, Option D fallback); custom contrasts and
  ordered factors refuse until the representation IR exists.
- **Stage 1 INLA-mapping** = refuse for new term classes unless
  test arbitration proves faithful mapping. The merged-v2 §3.4
  verification policy is the generic conditional-INLA gate for
  every new term class after v0.2.5.
- **Stage 2 effort acceptance** = 16--27 person-days; Stage 1C
  representation benchmarks are not droppable.
- **Stage 2 MVP partition** = 4 deliverables in v0.3.0 + 4
  follow-on in v0.3.1 (not all 8 in one v0.3.0 cycle).
- **`.fb_dataset()` export gate** = internal-only at v0.3.0;
  export only after at least two stable workflows prove the
  contract.
- **Stage 3A aggregation scope** = gaussian identity only; no
  smooths; no random slopes. Heterogeneous residual aggregation
  only with an explicit sufficient-statistics proof.
- **Version-bump policy** = clean release tag at every stage
  close (v0.2.6, v0.3.0, ...); development continues as `.9000`
  after each tag.
- **Memory-table vignette freeze** = at v0.2.6 close, but only
  after benchmark-backed values exist. The paper can cite the
  frozen vignette; paper deadlines must not distort the package
  roadmap.

### One design amendment — the Stage 3B output format

The v2.1 fix pass left Stage 3B's file-backed output defaulting
to csv + rds with `fst` deferred to a future Suggests. The
decision-answers reply pushed back: the deferral was a
dependency-cost guard, not a structural rejection, and the use
case — a chunked prediction emitting prediction grids at
$N \geq 10^6$ — is exactly the shape `fst` is designed for.
A benchmark was requested before finalising the policy.

The benchmark (script at `tools/benchmark_fst_stage3b_2026-05-23.R`;
persisted at `benchmark_results/fst_stage3b_2026-05-23.{csv,rds,log}`)
measured single-run round-trip wall-time and on-disk size at
$N \in \{10^5, 10^6, 5 \times 10^6, 10^7\}$ for csv
(`data.table::fwrite` defaults), rds (`base::saveRDS` defaults),
and fst (`fst::write_fst`, `compress = 50`). The Stage-3B-shape
grid carried six columns: an integer id, a factor `group` with
1000 levels, a numeric covariate `x`, and three numeric output
columns (`point`, `lower`, `upper`).

| N | format | write (s) | read (s) | on-disk (MB) |
|---:|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| $10^5$ | csv | 0.007 | 0.005 | 8.0 |
| $10^5$ | rds | 0.124 | 0.009 | 3.3 |
| $10^5$ | fst | 0.004 | 0.001 | 3.4 |
| $10^6$ | csv | 0.056 | 0.046 | 81.1 |
| $10^6$ | rds | 1.210 | 0.090 | 33.1 |
| $10^6$ | fst | 0.029 | 0.024 | 33.5 |
| $5 \times 10^6$ | csv | 0.278 | 0.179 | 409.8 |
| $5 \times 10^6$ | rds | 6.024 | 0.393 | 165.3 |
| $5 \times 10^6$ | fst | 0.156 | 0.079 | 167.2 |
| $10^7$ | csv | 0.547 | 0.342 | 820.6 |
| $10^7$ | rds | 12.148 | 0.787 | 330.6 |
| $10^7$ | fst | 0.309 | 0.127 | 334.4 |

Three findings drove the policy. First, rds and fst compress to
within 1% of the same on-disk size at every $N$ tier — the
compression argument for fst over rds is null. Second, fst
writes 30--40$\times$ faster than rds at $N \geq 10^6$ (at
$N = 10^7$: 0.31 s vs 12.15 s); read is 3--6$\times$ faster on
the same range. In a chunked predict loop emitting 100 chunks,
the rds path is 20 minutes of pure I/O and the fst path is 30
seconds. Third, csv is 2.4$\times$ larger on disk than fst/rds
at every $N$ tier and loses factor types — interop currency
costs disk space and round-trip semantics, an explicit trade,
not a default.

ADR 0023 absorbs the policy. `fst >= 0.9.0` lands in
`DESCRIPTION:Suggests` at v0.3.3, gated by
`requireNamespace("fst", quietly = TRUE)`. The default
`format = "auto"` resolves on $N$, fst availability, and an
interoperability flag; an explicit `format = "fst"` with `fst`
not installed raises a structured refusal naming
`install.packages("fst")` and offering a one-line override to
fall back to rds. No silent fall-back. The discipline matches
the package's broader posture from ADR 0017 (gate truth = emit
truth) and the G2--G4 governance gates: refusals are explicit
and informative; silent re-routes are forbidden.

### A note on methodology

The episode is a small one but illustrates how planning
decisions get made on this project. The starting position
(`fst` deferred to future Suggests) was conservative and
defensible. A pushback on dependency philosophy was raised; the
response was to run a numerical experiment on the actual use-
case shape rather than re-argue from first principles; the
experiment took five minutes of wall-time and produced an
unambiguous answer. ADR 0023 cites the experiment by file, not
by re-derivation, so future readers can re-run the script if
the platform or fst version changes. This is the same pattern
applied to G2 (`prior_fixed_sd = 100`, ADR 0010), G3
(`backend = "auto"`, ADR 0006), and the smooth-prediction bug
(ADR 0018): a position is held until a numerical observation
forces an update, then the update lands with the observation
attached as evidence.

## The path to v1.0

| Milestone | Posture | Calendar (parallel-pace baseline) |
|---|---|---|
| v0.2.5 | Hardening; no new user surface. | Q3 2026 |
| v0.3.0 -- v0.3.2 | AAGI Symposium November 2026 deliverable band. | November 2026 |
| v0.3.3 -- v0.3.6 | Chunked prediction, backend routing, structured-cov priors, tensor smooths. | 2027 (parallel pace) |
| v0.4.0 | Approximation registry + scaling claim. | Q1 2028 (parallel pace) |
| v0.9 | Release rehearsal; lift exports from experimental to maturing. | TBD post-v0.4 |
| v1.0 | Stable; core exports promoted. | TBD post-v0.9 |

The release cadence is intentionally measured. Each minor
release earns its place by closing a defined set of items
rather than by hitting a calendar date. The parallel-pace lock
in November 2026 stretches the v0.4.0 horizon from the earlier
Q1 2027 anchor to roughly Q1 2028; the §9.2 review checkpoints
in the merged-v2 plan refresh the next-stage date at each
stage close.

# Governance, reproducibility, and the collaborative model

## The AAGI-AUS collective

flexyBayes is an AAGI-AUS collective effort. The `CITATION.cff`
and `DESCRIPTION` files name four coauthors: Max Moldovan
(creator + author), Emi Tanaka (author), Francis K.C. Hui
(author), Beata Sznajder (author). The methods paper coauthor
list (decision D5), the paper venue (D10), the upstream rename
(D8), and the timing of Stage 4 (the rename milestone) are
collective decisions deferred to a team conversation; they are
not single-author calls.

The artefact carries multiple contributors with explicit roles,
the deferred decisions are documented as deferred to a named
group, and the conversation that resolves them is a planned
event rather than an after-the-fact rationalisation.

## Reproducibility commitments

- *Pinned-version snapshots.* `renv` is supported on the
  development side; `CITATION.cff` carries the version and
  release date; `codemeta.json` carries the SoftwareSourceCode
  metadata. Production users who need stability pin to a
  specific 0.2.x patch (see `API_STABILITY.md`).
- *Random-seed discipline.* `flexybayes()` and `fb_brms()`
  accept a `seed` argument; greta's MCMC threads it through to
  TensorFlow Probability; brms threads it through to Stan. The
  `review_code` workflow snapshots `.Random.seed` so a direct
  call and a review-then-proceed pair reproduce the same R-RNG
  state.
- *Cross-engine verification.* Fits are verified against
  external references (`lme4::lmer`, `mgcv::gam`, `INLA::inla`
  direct) on every meaningful change. The verification lives in
  the test suite rather than in a one-off notebook.
- *Sustained development history.* Thirty-five commits across
  six weeks of development, conventional-commits style themed
  by area (`feat(api):`, `test:`, `docs(release):`, etc.). The
  public history will become visible when the upstream rename
  ships.

## Open-source practices

- *Test discipline.* Three tiers documented in
  `CONTRIBUTING.md` with the exact commands and the expected
  PASS / FAIL / SKIP counts per tier.
- *Documentation tiers.* README for the overview; twelve
  numbered vignettes for the tutorial deck; pkgdown for the API
  reference; `NEWS.md` for the release diary; `API_STABILITY.md`
  for the lifecycle ladder; this narrative for the development
  walkthrough.
- *Lifecycle clarity.* Every export is
  `lifecycle::badge("experimental")` at v0.2.x; the promotion
  ladder reaches "maturing" at v0.9. Deprecations follow
  `lifecycle::deprecate_warn()` cycles of at least one minor
  release.
- *Governance documents.* `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md`,
  `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `SUPPORT.md` ship with the
  repository. Items pending the collective decision are flagged
  as `Pending AAGI-AUS collective decision` rather than as
  TODOs.

## Evaluation framework

A committee evaluating the package against the four standard
software-paper criteria can locate the evidence as follows.

1. *Research impact.* Documented in §2. The user community
   (agricultural-statistics and the broader Bayesian-mixed-
   model crowd) is real and is presently served by single-
   backend tools. The triangulation diagnostic is a contribution
   distinct from any single engine.
2. *Design rationale.* Eighteen ADRs in
   `design-notes-priors-brms-lgm.md`, each with a four-point
   justification including literature anchoring and sensitivity
   bracketing. The four-verb scope is enforced.
3. *Open-source practices.* Three-tier test discipline; CRAN-
   ready `R CMD check --as-cran` baseline; vignette precompile
   pattern; governance documents; lifecycle ladder.
4. *Development authenticity.* Six weeks of concentrated work,
   thirty-five commits, eighteen ADRs, two independent audits
   driving substantial rework, four named coauthors with defined
   paper-contribution roles. Decisions are deferred to the
   collective rather than stamped by the lead.

The development model is structured: plan, decide (ADR),
implement, audit, revise, document. The sections above record
that cadence end to end.

# Appendix A — code snippets

The package code is at `flexyBayes/` in this workspace. Four
snippets below illustrate the patterns described in §6.

## A.1 The four-verb decision

```r
library(flexyBayes)
data(sleepstudy, package = "lme4")

# (a) ASReml-style entry
fit_a <- flexybayes(
  fixed  = Reaction ~ Days,
  random = ~ Subject,
  data   = sleepstudy,
  backend = "auto"             # gate-driven INLA or greta
)
backend_decision(fit_a)

# (b) brms / lme4 entry with the Stan passthrough
fit_b <- fb_brms(
  Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject),
  data = sleepstudy,
  backend = "brms"             # explicit Stan via brms
)

# (c) Cross-engine triangulation
triangulate(fit_a, fit_b)
```

## A.2 The LGM gate refusal template

```r
# A structurally-incompatible model: family outside INLA's roster.
fb_bad <- flexyBayes:::fb_from_asreml(
  fixed = y ~ x, random = ~ g,
  data  = data.frame(y = rnorm(20),
                     x = rnorm(20),
                     g = factor(rep(1:4, 5))),
  family = "imaginary_family"
)

ref <- flexyBayes:::lgm_gate(fb_bad)
ref
#> flexyBayes: INLA backend refused for this model.
#> Reasons (1 structural failure):
#>   - [family_allowlist] family "imaginary_family" is not in the
#>     INLA likelihood allowlist (no built-in Laplace machinery).
#>     Diagnostic: fb$family = "imaginary_family"
#> Re-route: try backend = "brms" via fb_brms() for the Stan
#>   passthrough (model must be in the brms corpus), or
#>   backend = "greta" for the broader flexyBayes formula path.
#>   NIMBLE is planned future work, not yet implemented.
#> For mixtures with <= 2 components, the planned INLA-within-MCMC
#>   escape (Gomez-Rubio & Rue 2018) is on the roadmap.
#> Override (not recommended): lgm_gate(fb, force = "inla",
#>   acknowledge_silent_bias_risk = TRUE, reason = "<your reason>")
#> Docs: vignette("flexyBayes-11-lgm-feasibility").
```

## A.3 The canonical-name registry on an INLA fit

```r
fit_inla <- flexybayes(Reaction ~ Days, random = ~ Subject,
                       data = sleepstudy, backend = "inla")

canonical_names(fit_inla)
#>   native                                     canonical      transform
#>   "(Intercept)"                              "(Intercept)"  identity
#>   "Days"                                     "Days"         identity
#>   "Precision for Subject"                    "sd_Subject"   1/sqrt(.)
#>   "Precision for the Gaussian observations" "sigma"        1/sqrt(.)
```

## A.4 The prior DSL

```r
# PC-canonical SD-scale prior DSL. The PC idiom is the cross-engine
# interlingua; the distributional idiom is engine-direct.
my_prior <- fb_prior(
  sigma                 ~ pc(upper = 2, prob = 0.05),
  sd(group = "Subject") ~ half_normal(scale = 1),
  b("Days")             ~ student_t(df = 4, scale = 2.5)
)

# Inspect the resolved prior at fit time
fit <- flexybayes(Reaction ~ Days, random = ~ Subject,
                  data = sleepstudy, prior = my_prior)
prior_summary(fit)
```
